transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-29
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (recording)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Derek Shaw (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Montclair - Platform), Tom Reyes (Montclair - CTO), Lena Ortiz (Montclair - Data Privacy), Raj (engineer)

Summary:
Quick kickoff/demo to show schema-first "JSON mode" workflows in Console and API, discuss guardrails for tool-calling and structured outputs, and confirm pilot scope and security requirements for a Montclair Health POC. Customer is particularly sensitive to data residency, KMS/bring-your-own-key, and auditability.

Topics:
- JSON mode / schema enforcement in Redwood Console and API
- Tool/function calling patterns (EHR connector, ticketing, and audit log sink)
- Runtime guardrails and fallback orchestration
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs VPC/private deployment options for PHI
- Pilot scope and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: ok hi everyone, thanks for carving out time today. i'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. i think we have 45-ish minutes... looks like 52 on the calendar, so we'll use it. Derek's with me, our SE, and we'll walk through a schema-first example and then talk next steps for a pilot.
[00:20] Tom: hey thanks. short intro from our side — i'm Tom, cto. Aisha is our platform lead, Lena covers privacy/compliance, and Raj is one of our platform engineers.
[00:30] Aisha: yep thanks. our main ask, quick: we need a deterministic structured output for clinical metadata extraction and safe tool calls into our ticketing system. also need to understand exactly how data leaves our VPC, if at all.
[00:44] Derek: totally. we'll demo JSON mode (schema enforcement) in the console and the API, show how you can pin a schema, validate at runtime, and then wire a function call to your EHR connector or internal ticketing. i'll also show the fallback behavior when the model doesn't comply with the schema.
[00:58] Lena: and security: we need KMS integration for keys, audit logs that show token-level details, and SOC 2 type 2 evidence. we also have data residency constraints — some payloads must stay in us-east and not be exported.
[01:12] Maya: great notes. quick agenda: 1) brief UX demo (console) of schema-first prompts + tool calls, 2) a sample API call showing the same, 3) discuss deployments and security, 4) confirm pilot scoping. sound good?
[01:22] Tom: yes, go ahead.

--- Demo start ---
[01:30] Derek: i'm sharing screen now. ok console home, i open the schema playground — note this is a saved workspace we can export. here i've uploaded a schema that looks like a nested JSON: patient.id, encounter.date, findings[].code, severity enum, and a metadata.audit object. the schema enforces types and required fields.
[02:05] Derek: when i run an example prompt the runtime will validate the model output against the schema before returning to the caller. if validation fails, we have two policies: 1) soft-fail — return the unvalidated content with a warning, 2) strict — post-validation, the runtime triggers a corrective re-prompt or routes to a fallback model/tool. i'll flip to strict so you see the enforcement flow.
[02:35] Aisha: in strict mode, is it re-asking the model or calling a tool to repair? what's the delta for latency?
[02:42] Derek: good q. we support both. most customers do a corrective re-prompt (we append the failed fields and ask for exact JSON per schema) which adds another roundtrip. p95 for an average corrective flow on our Dedicated instance for 512 tokens was ~180-240ms extra per correction in our benchmarks, depends on model and batch. alternative is routing to a deterministic extractor tool you own — that trades off latency for determinism.
[03:08] Raj: when you say batch, i assume you mean continuous batching at runtime? how does that interact with low-latency strict mode?
[03:16] Derek: yes continuous batching is on by default but the serving runtime respects latency SLOs. for strict mode we can set a lower batching window or pin to a lower-concurrency pool to avoid added latency. that's part of the Dedicated config we can tune.

[03:40] Derek: i'll demonstrate a tool call now — in this example the model returns a JSON action: {"action":"create_ticket","ticket":{"summary":"Patient allergy mismatch","severity":"high"}} and Redwood will call a configured function (we call them tools) that posts to your internal ticket API. you can add an approval step, add RBAC enforcement, and we surface the full execution trace in the Console.
[04:10] Aisha: is the function invocation proxied through Redwood, or does it make a server-side call from our VPC? we can't have PII leave our environment without encryption + BYOK.
[04:20] Derek: two options. Hosted API option proxies calls via Redwood with end-to-end TLS and supports customer-managed KMS for payload sealing, but the default still touches our control plane. Dedicated or Private (VPC) deployments let you run the function wiring in your network — the runtime can be deployed to your VPC and calls never exit your subnet. for PHI we'd recommend Dedicated + VPC/private connector.
[04:48] Lena: and the audit logs?
[04:50] Derek: audit logs include timestamped events for every request, the schema validation result, tool invocation payloads (redacted per policy), and a token-level cost/latency breakdown. we also have an immutable audit sink to S3 or your SIEM.

[05:10] Maya: sharing a link in chat to our security pack — you'll see SOC2 Type II, ISO evidence, and KMS integration docs. also sending the schema playbook we used in the demo: [link] drive.google.com/redwood/schema-playbook (note: placeholder).

[05:35] Tom: nice. can you show how fallback orchestration works? for example, if the primary model hallucinates a value, can we fallback to a smaller model or a rule-based extractor?
[05:46] Derek: absolutely. i'll flip to the orchestration tab — you can configure routing policies: prefer low-cost model A for most traffic, but if schema validation fails or confidence is low, route to a "safe" variant (more deterministic) or a bespoke extractor. we also have a canary rollout and A/B rules so you can test behavioral regressions. here's an example policy: primary -> gpt-like-open (fast) ; on validation fail -> bert-extractor (deterministic) ; if extractor fails -> human-in-the-loop ticket.
[06:22] Raj: how do you detect confidence? is it model-provided or a Redwood metric?
[06:27] Derek: we compute hybrid signals: model token-level probabilities, schema-violation counts, and semantic similarity to expected enums. threshold triggers are configurable.

[06:40] Maya: quick pause — any other architecture or security blockers we should know now?
[06:47] Aisha: data residency: some data must stay us-east; can you guarantee region pinning for model hosting and logs?
[06:54] Derek: yes region pinning is supported for Dedicated and Private so all inference, KV cache, and logs can remain in us-east. Hosted tier can be region-selected but it's a shared infra; for strict residency Dedicated is recommended.

[07:10] Tom: okay, practical pilot scope? we want to run a 2-week pilot that ingests ~10k records, tests schema enforcement across 5 templates, and validates tool calls into our jira-like system and audit sink. estimate cost and how long to provision?
[07:24] Maya: we can provision a trial Dedicated pool for the pilot — typically 3-5 days to stand up depending on networking. cost estimate i can send after i confirm pool size; we'll base on throughput needs.
[07:35] Derek: for 10k records with an average output size of 300 tokens, continuous batching and caching can give sizable unit-cost reductions; we'll produce a draft benchmark sheet.

[07:50] Derek: now i want to show the API call parity — same schema enforcement exists in the API: you POST a schema + prompt and set validation_policy=strict. sample curl:
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \\
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \\
 -d '{"model":"redwood-aurora","schema":"/schemas/clinical-v1.json","validation":"strict","prompt":"extract clinical findings"}'

[08:30] Aisha: small nit — do you version schemas? we need change control and history for audits.
[08:34] Derek: yes every schema is versioned, and the Console shows a schema diff and who published it. rollbacks are single-click, and you can pin a specific schema version to a route.

[08:50] Tom: can the model write nested objects reliably? e.g., a findings array with code, loinc mapping, and evidence text?
[08:58] Derek: in our experience with schema enforcement and corrective prompts we've seen very high compliance for nested structures — but we recommend an extractor tool for deterministic LOINC mapping. combination pattern is common: model extracts free text into structured fields, then you run a deterministic mapping tool to canonicalize codes.

[09:20] Lena: what about PII redaction? we need to ensure PHI is redacted before logs are stored in long-term storage.
[09:28] Derek: we have a redaction policy layer that can scrub fields per schema flags before writing to audit sinks. you can set fields as sensitive and they will be redacted or tokenized.

[09:40] Derek: i'll now flip to a live run where the model intentionally emits malformed JSON (common transcription demo). watch the schema validator catch a missing required field and trigger a corrective re-prompt.
[09:55] Derek: run 1 — model returns malformed ("findings": "n/a"), validator flags, corrective re-prompt appended: "Return only JSON valid to schema clinical-v1.json. missing fields: findings[].code, severity." run 2 — model returns corrected JSON. you can see the trace in the Console with timestamps and regenerated tokens.
[10:25] Raj: curious — can we route the corrective attempt to a different model automatically?
[10:29] Derek: yes that's just an orchestration rule: on validation fail route to extractor-model-1. we can also set max retries and then fall back to human approval.

[10:45] Tom: what about function/tool secrets — we don't want Redwood to hold service account keys.
[10:52] Maya: good point — for hosted we support scoped short-lived credentials and encrypted secrets with customer-managed KMS; for Dedicated/Private you can host secrets in your KMS and the runtime retrieves them inside your VPC.

[11:10] Aisha: ok let's talk about telemetry and cost visibility — we need token-level cost breakdowns per route and per schema for internal chargebacks.
[11:18] Derek: Console exposes token breakdown, per-route cost, and trace-level latency. Optimize (our recommendations product) will suggest batching/window sizes and quantization profiles and estimate unit-cost savings. we'll attach a sample Optimize report to the follow-up.

[11:40] Maya: quick check — any blockers for the pilot timeline (Dec 6 week)?
[11:45] Tom: network approvals and sign-off on privacy controls are the only gating items; Lena will confirm.
[11:50] Lena: i'll need to see the SOC2 docs and the redaction policy; i also want to run a short legal review.
[11:57] Maya: understood — i'll send docs. Derek will provision a sample repo and schema templates.

[12:10] Derek: last demo bit — tool execution traces include the raw request/response (redacted), a unique correlation id, and an execution timeline. this is helpful for debugging failed tool calls. we also log the model prompt, but you can opt to not persist prompts in long-term storage for privacy.
[12:35] Raj: do you support HL7-ish payloads? we won't transform to JSON upstream in time for pilot.
[12:41] Derek: yes we can ingest HL7 and run a transformation extractor as a preprocessor tool, or you can upload a transformer that runs in your VPC. both patterns are used.

[12:55] Tom: anything else on architecture?
[12:58] Derek: only note: caching — we support prefix and KV caching. for repeated reports we can cache token sequences to reduce cost and latency. but for PHI you can configure cache eviction and disable persistent caching.

[13:15] Maya: signposting next steps: we'll send the security pack, schema templates, a draft pilot runbook, and a benchmark worksheet. propose pilot week of Dec 6; Derek to spin up trial environment once we get network details.
[13:30] Tom: sounds good. can you confirm the expected provisioning time?
[13:33] Derek: once we receive networking info 48–72 hours for a trial Dedicated, sometimes quicker if we can use an existing peering.

[13:50] Aisha: ok one more question — if downstream ticketing has a strict schema, can we validate before calling the ticketing API to avoid failed requests?
[13:58] Derek: yes you can chain schemas — validate model output against clinical-v1, then run a transformer that shapes to your ticket schema and validate again before invoking. errors can be surfaced as warnings or block calls entirely.

[14:15] Lena: for legal we need to know retention defaults — default audit retention is how long?
[14:21] Derek: default is 90 days in hosted, but Dedicated can be configured to your retention policy and we can export to your S3 for long-term archiving.

[14:35] Maya: wrapping up — recap: 1) we demonstrated schema-first JSON mode and corrective/fallback flows; 2) tool calling with VPC/private options for PHI; 3) audit logs and KMS/BYOK patterns; 4) pilot proposal week of Dec 6 to validate with 10k records.
[14:58] Tom: agreed. Lena will do a legal/privacy check; Aisha will share payload samples.
[15:05] Maya: great — i'll follow up with the security bundle and the sample schemas. Derek will attach the sample project and the benchmark worksheet.
[15:14] Aisha: can you also include an example of the Console export we can drop into our CI for nightly validation?
[15:19] Derek: yes will include the CI export script.
[15:22] Tom: ok thanks everyone.
[15:25] Maya: thanks all, we'll email next steps and proposed calendar invites.

[15:35] (meeting ends, recording stops)
